I moved to São Paulo for the cursinho. As a result, I stopped training completely.
Let me play devil’s advocate for a minute. You were good at basketball, really good. Why throw that away for six years of medical school?
I did not throw it away. To be fair, basketball gave me everything I know about discipline. That being said, I could not see myself doing it at thirty-five.
Plenty of people coach at thirty-five. That is a career too. What is your counterargument to that?
Coaching is a good career. However, it is not the one I want. What’s more, medicine uses the part of the game I liked most: deciding fast, under pressure.
Okay, but that undermines your point a little, doesn’t it? If you like pressure, sport has plenty of it.
Granted, it does. Even so, in medicine the pressure is about somebody else, not about me. As a result, it feels like it matters more.
That is a real stance, and I cannot rebut it. Would you still say it at two in the morning, after a thirty-hour shift?
Ask me again in six years. But yes, I think I would stand by it. And you — was there ever a decision you had to defend like this?

I coached school debate for twelve years, and the first thing I taught every new student was not how to attack. It was how to agree. Most beginners think the strongest argument is the one that admits nothing. In fact, it is the weakest, because the judge can see the point you are hiding from. So we practiced one move until it was automatic. You name the best thing the other side has said, out loud and fairly. To be fair, they are right that the exam is objective. Then you pause. And then you turn it. That being said, an objective exam can still measure the wrong thing. The pause matters as much as the words. Students who rushed it sounded defensive. Students who took their time sounded like they had already considered everything, which, by the end of the season, they usually had.

Every year somebody asks me whether a single entrance exam is a fair way to choose future doctors. My honest answer is that it depends on what you mean by fair. On the one hand, it treats every candidate the same way. Nobody gets in because of who their parents know, and that matters in a country like ours. On the other hand, the same test rewards the students who could afford two years of preparation, which means that equal rules do not always produce equal chances. Some universities abroad try to solve this with interviews and personal essays. However, those methods bring their own problems, because they are easier to coach and harder to check. As a result, I no longer believe there is a perfect system. What I do believe is that anybody who defends one without admitting its weakness has not thought about it for very long.
